text: US | adopted, effective ~60 days after FR publication. FAA now requires every radio altimeter on Part 91 aircraft flying in CONUS+DC to tolerate neighbouring-band wireless signals in 3.7-4.2 GHz. Airlines (Part 121) and large foreign carriers (Part 129) must comply by 30 Dec 2030, one day before FCC permits new Upper C-band service; everyone else by 31 Oct 2034. FAA can regulate only the aircraft, not the wireless emissions environment.

US | analysis. FAA checked its tolerance mask against FCC limits at a 35 ft separation from a base station. Adjacent-band fundamental: 65 dBm/MHz EIRP -> 0.4 dBW/m2/MHz at 35 ft, +6 dB margin = 6.4, mask 9.5. In-band spurious: -28.4 dBm/MHz EIRP -> -93 dBW/m2/MHz, +6 dB margin +5 dB aggregation = -82, mask -82 (zero residual headroom beyond the stated margins). Useful as a worked template for a simulator's margin calculation.

US | FCC order as described by FAA. New Upper C-band wireless: 3980-4140 MHz, guard 4140-4160, FSS repack 4160-4200; CONUS+DC only; earliest service 31 Dec 2030; base-station EIRP up to 65 dBm/MHz; antenna height up to 450 ft AGL; unwanted emissions into 4200-4400 MHz capped at -28.4 dBm/MHz EIRP (dual-pol) or -46 dBm/MHz conducted. Lower C-band cap into the RA band tightened from -13 to the same new limit.

US | voluntary. Since before mid-2023, Lower C-band carriers have voluntarily coordinated power and limited emissions near airports through 1 Jan 2028; major carriers offered to extend to the Upper C-band start date (31 Dec 2030). These are commitments, not statutes - a policy agent should treat them as non-binding but relied-upon mitigations. US mitigations summarized by ICAO include limits on antenna elevation above the horizon and tower coordination near airports.

Safety reasoning pattern. Radio-altimeter data feeds autoland, CAT II/III, terrain warning, collision avoidance, windshear and rotorcraft automation, and the pilot may not detect bad data. FAA evaluates worst-case compliant base-station layouts: one critical site under a flight path near an airport drives the risk; safety is not averaged across locations. ICAO Doc 9718 advises 6-10 dB margin for aeronautical safety systems.

India | published, effective 31 Dec 2027 (NOT yet in force on 7 Oct 2026). DGCA order in AIC 19/2025: radio altimeters cannot be relied upon if exposed to 5G C-band (3.3-3.67 GHz in India). Applies to all airplanes with RA. After the effective date, non-tolerant airplanes may not fly ILS, SA CAT I/II, CAT II/III, autoland, HUD-to-touchdown or EFVS-to-touchdown in Indian airspace. Tolerant aircraft need no action. No numeric tolerance threshold appears in the appendix.

India | published, effective 31 Dec 2027. Rotorcraft with non-tolerant altimeters may not use RA-minimum offshore approaches (use barometric), RA-dependent hover or SAR autopilot modes, or takeoff/landing procedures (Cat A/B, performance class) that require RA data. Tolerant rotorcraft: no action.

India | secondary, low reliability. Press reports DGCA restrictions on 3.3 GHz 5G near airports and operators asking for an 18-month fleet retrofit deadline; a trade report describes a 19 Nov 2025 DGCA order with a 31 Dec 2027 deadline. The primary AIC text expresses this as limitations on non-tolerant aircraft. No primary document with airport buffer distances or power limits was located: treat that as an open gap.

India | inference. India's auctioned 5G C-band (3300-3670 MHz) ends 530 MHz below the 4200 MHz altimeter band, versus 220 MHz for US Lower C-band, so unwanted-emission and blocking risk is expected to be lower than the US case. But DGCA still treats the band as a hazard, and separation alone is not a regulatory exemption.

International | in force. 4200-4400 MHz is reserved for aircraft radio altimeters (and associated ground transponders) under footnote 5.438. RR 4.10 says safety services need special measures against harmful interference. Therefore no 5G carrier or emission may be authorized inside 4200-4400 MHz, and network changes near aircraft must be evaluated for out-of-band and blocking effects.

3GPP band plan. n78 = 3300-3800 MHz (India's 3300-3670 allocation sits inside it), n77 = 3300-4200 MHz, n79 = 4400-5000 MHz. In the US, n77 is restricted to 3450-3550 and 3700-3980 MHz. A device or radio unit supporting n77 up to 4200 MHz is not thereby authorized to transmit there; authorization is national.

Europe | published Nov 2024. ECC Report 362 finds 3400-3800 MHz 5G emissions leave at least 6 dB margin in a modelled ILS approach; fully covered for base stations >1200 m from threshold or >40 m laterally, or with improved unwanted-emission levels. Tests found no interference in the scenarios and aircraft tried; only UC1 altimeters were modelled.

Europe | disputed. EASA says ECC 362 does not justify a fleet-wide retrofit regulation, preferring case-by-case corrective action; aviation interests and EUROCONTROL's 2024 study say interference cannot be excluded for all combinations. Retain both views; do not average them.

ICAO | guidance. Mitigation menu from ICAO MID/FSMP material: power limits, downward antenna tilt, spectrum separation, precautionary or exclusion zones, and consultation with aviation regulators before enabling 5G; propagation modelling per ITU-R P.528. Status as a final ICAO circular unconfirmed.

US | in force. FAA AD 2023-10-02 defines altimeter tolerance by PSD thresholds for fundamental (3.7-3.98 GHz) and spurious (4.2-4.4 GHz) emissions; non-tolerant airplanes may not perform certain RA-dependent operations where NOTAMs identify 5G interference. NOTAM is the operational trigger linking network deployments to aircraft restrictions.
Protection-area analysis considers aircraft geometry and height, 5G base-station characteristics, and air-to-ground propagation.

Cells appear as NRCellDU (admin/operational/usage state, configuredMaxTxPower attribute); transmit resources as NRSectorCarrier (direction, ARFCN, bandwidth). Load is observed through TS 28.552 PRB measurements: usage distribution, peak DL/UL PRBs used, available PRBs, MIMO-aware usage, and per-SSB-beam usage, which 3GPP positions as input for load balancing and coverage reshaping.
